title: Paul and James reconciled: no legal perfect works vs no bare assent without works
source_text: XXXIX. Atque hinc sese aperit via commoda & facilis conciliandi Paulum cum Jacobo, qui in speciem Paulo contradicit. Paulus enim, ut jam vidimus, affirmat Deum credenti imputare justitiam sine operibus, & justificare eum qui credit, & non operatur; & multis in locis vehementer contendit hominem justificari per fidem sine operibus legis. Jacobus vero contra disertis verbis asserit, & multis argumentis probat, quod ex operibus justificatur homo, & non ex fide tantum. Sed quamvis eorum verba videantur inter se pugnare, sensus tamen optime concordat. Paulus enim negare vult hominem justificari faciendo opera, quae lex, ut foederi gratiae opposita, exigit ad hominis justificationem: quod Jacobus minime affirmat. Jacobus autem asserere intendit, hominem non justificari solo & nudo assensu qui verbo Evangelii adhibetur, sed fide tali quae sit per dilectionem operans, & quam multa bona opera comitentur, quod Paulus ipse expresse docuit, tantum abest ut illud neget. Adeoque, quum dicit Jacobus, Videtis igitur ex operibus justificari hominem, & non ex fide tantum, idem est ac si diceret, Videtis Deum pro justo non habere illum qui verbo Dei simpliciter & nude credit & assentitur: sed illum qui cum fide conjungit bona opera, & qui fidem habet in bonis operibus efficacem.
pass_a_gloss: And from this opens a convenient and easy way of reconciling Paul with James, who in appearance contradicts Paul. For Paul, as we have already seen, affirms that God imputes righteousness to the believer without works and justifies the one who believes and does not work; and in many places vehemently contends that a person is justified through faith without works of the law. James on the contrary asserts in express words and proves by many arguments that a person is justified from works and not from faith only. But although their words seem to fight each other, their sense nevertheless agrees excellently. For Paul wants to deny that a person is justified by doing the works which the law, as opposed to the covenant of grace, requires for a person's justification—which James by no means affirms. But James intends to assert that a person is not justified by the sole and bare assent given to the word of the Gospel, but by such faith as works through love and which many good works accompany—which Paul himself expressly taught, so far is he from denying it. And so when James says, You see then that a person is justified from works and not from faith only, it is the same as if he said: You see that God does not hold as just the one who simply and barely believes and assents to God's word, but the one who joins good works with faith and has a faith effective in good works.
pass_b_english: Paul denies justification by law-covenant perfect works; James denies bare gospel assent.
Both require living love-working faith—James's 'not faith only' matches Paul's own teaching.

choices.why: James excludes idle assent, not Paul's living faith.
